## Traditional Toughness
When college students were asked to describe toughness they offered hard-nosed, gritty, playing through pain, stoic, emotional fortitude, showing no signs of distress, persevering. Among 160 elite athletes perseverance came out on top. The image that arises is a football player popping a dislocated shoulder back in and demanding to return, or Craig MacTavish who retired in 1997 as the last NHL player to play without a helmet, or a wounded military hero or a mother fighting through discomfort to care for her child. Traditionally toughness is overcoming obstacles with perseverance, discipline and stoicism, often pictured as a strong brute of a man.

## Bobby Knight and Old-School Coaching
Bobby Knight’s career spanned five decades and three universities: more than nine hundred wins, third most all-time in college basketball, five Final Fours, three NCAA national championships. His 1976 Indiana team won every game, sweeping the NCAA tournament with a win over Michigan for a perfect season and Knight’s first title. Knight later said: “That was a team that was almost impossible to beat, because of its toughness, its strength, its size.”

For a man who began at West Point toughness was “Being able to overcome obstacles. You can’t feel sorry for yourself.” The team lived it with disciplined, hard-nosed basketball, pioneering a pressing man-to-man defense that tested discipline, work ethic and perseverance.

The problem was the methods. Knight is known as much for winning as for tantrums and abusive antics. There were tampons hanging from lockers of players he thought were “soft,” frequent cussing out of players, accusations he ordered managers to tape pictures of women’s genitalia in players’ rooms. The 1991 tape: “This is absolute fucking bullshit. Now I’ll fucking run your ass right into the ground… I had to sit around for a fucking year with an 8–10 record in this fucking league, and I mean you will not put me in that fucking position again or you will goddamn pay for it like you can’t fucking believe.” He brought a piece of toilet paper covered in shit to show players what he thought of them, and the infamous video of Knight choking a player at practice. All in the name of Knight’s version of toughness.

“Soft.” Female genitalia. Questioning manhood. These clue Knight’s actual definition: showing no weakness, bulldozing through obstacles, using fear to establish authority and control. Old-school, still dominant on playing fields and in performance halls.

## Tough Parenting
Diana Baumrind in the 1960s classified parenting by responsiveness and demandingness. Responsiveness is “the extent to which parents intentionally foster individuality, self-regulation, and self-assertion by being attuned, supportive, and acquiescent to children’s special needs and demands.” Demandingness is “the claims parents make on children to become integrated into the family whole, by their maturity demands, supervision, disciplinary efforts and willingness to confront the child who disobeys.”

Low demandingness/high responsiveness = permissive, too soft. High demandingness/low responsiveness = authoritarian, too hard, harsh discipline with little attention to needs.

Authoritarian parents don’t trust children to make good decisions. The parent is in charge, child obeys, via fear, threats, punishment. Refrain: “You need to do this because I said so.” In a study of over one thousand parents only 31 percent of authoritarian parents said they should “love their child unconditionally.” Motivation is sticks not carrots.

They jump to criticism after a missed shot, ground a kid after a subpar test score and lock them in a room to study with only “work harder.” Fathers who perceive their role as to “toughen up” their boys command them to suck it up, don’t cry, grow up, never show fear. In one study 81 percent of Americans thought parents were too soft.

Punishment or “work harder” doesn’t always work, and when demandingness far outweighs support you get authoritarian parenting. The Goldilocks fit is high expectations with warmth and understanding. The same principles hold for how we treat each other; we kept the demanding part and forgot warmth, care and responsiveness.

## Callousness and Machismo
Callous means to harden, make insensitive, develop thick skin. Language around toughness calls teams “soft,” urges them to “harden up,” to “show no signs of weakness.” The Karate Kid narrative is romanticized. In youth sports kids run laps or burpees not for training adaptation but to “toughen them up.” In *Until It Hurts*, Mark Hyman found frequent throwing up after workouts and insult-laden tirades. Parents justified teaching eleven-year-olds to go until they puke: “The stern approach is necessary for children to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior.”

For too long toughness meant thick skin, fear nothing, constrain emotional reaction, hide vulnerability: callous.

Toughness is tied to masculinity and machismo: “man up,” “stop being a pussy,” and *A League of Their Own*: “There’s no crying in baseball!” The image dominates: The Rock or Vin Diesel over a small female of similar prowess; brute strength with confidence and bravado. Women, research consistently shows, quietly handle pain better than men, and may have the correct definition based on reality not false confidence and bluster.

The old model is Bobby Knight coaching, authoritarian parents, callous leading. It’s the myth of an “inner warrior” built on callous demandingness, a remnant of military drill sergeants. Toughness has been hijacked; external displays are prioritized over true inner strength.

## Downfall of Callous View
On May 29, 2018, University of Maryland football ran ten 110-yard sprints. By number seven, 19-year-old Jordan McNair showed profound fatigue, bending over, cramping. Coaches and trainers goaded him: “get him the [expletive] up” and “drag his [expletive] across the field.” Video shows McNair surrounded by teammates aiding him at near-walking pace. After he complained of cramps it took trainers 34 minutes to have him taken off the field and another 28 minutes to call 911. One hour and 28 minutes elapsed between his final sprint and the ambulance. He died two weeks later from heatstroke, partly from a horrid medical response and an inability to separate pushing through pain from actual danger.

Rhabdomyolysis, or rhabdo, is damaged muscle products leaking into bloodstream, demanding kidneys process it; extreme cases can kill. Once rare from infections or drug use, it has become somewhat common from extreme workouts: endless push-ups, squats, burpees designed not to improve fitness but to test athletes. B. David Ridpath described it: “Taking a cue from a head coach with a desire to either toughen up the current players or weed out a few to open some scholarship slots, the strength coach often will ‘condition’ these players with a vengeance and a mandate to make them suffer.”

Authoritarian parenting leads to lower independence, more aggressive behavior, higher likelihood of substance abuse and risky behaviors. In sport it links to lower grit and increased emotional exhaustion, burnout, fear of failure. In a study of over 1,200 parents authoritarian parenting linked to higher child misbehavior. In the Israeli military those who grew up authoritarian adapted and coped with military life worse than peers from nurturing environments.

It creates fragile, dependent individuals. One young athlete said: “Coaches use exercise as punishment because they want you to become stronger… It gets in your head and you start thinking, ‘I need to do better. I need to work harder because I don’t want to be punished.’” He wanted to avoid punishment, not get better for internal reasons.

## Redefining Toughness
Trying to toughen through callousness trains response to fear and power. We push through discomfort because we imagine someone yelling or punishment looming. External facade “I’m not afraid of anything!” matters more than handling difficulty. Remove fear, power and control and the “tough” individual lacks skills to navigate adversity.

Fake toughness is easy to spot: Knight losing control in the name of discipline, appearance of power without substance, the gym bully, the executive masking insecurity by yelling, the strength coach causing injury, the parent confusing demandingness for discipline. Fake toughness is control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, based on appearance over substance.

Emerging science points to a different definition. Real toughness is experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, creating space to take thoughtful action. It’s maintaining a clear head to make the appropriate decision. Toughness is navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can.

Pete Carroll offers a contrast. He allows players to be who they are, celebrates “the way they see the world,” encourages meditation and yoga, shifts to ring toss if players get heated. A star player said: “He’s never negative, doesn’t scream. He finds a way to turn a mistake into a positive.”

After losing his NFL job in the 1990s Carroll stopped imitating others. He is one of only three coaches to win both an NCAA championship and a Super Bowl. He wants players who come through when the game is on the line, but believes toughness comes from inner drive, embracing challenges, bouncing back, perseverance and passion. He uses “always compete” practices but gives players skills to handle adversity: “Teaching guys how to feel confident enough to believe in what they’ve been prepared to do and believing what they can do and they go out there and do it.”

Carroll develops real toughness: control replaced with autonomy, appearance with substance, rigid pushing with flexibility, fear motivation with inner drive, insecurity with quiet confidence. Ken Reed summarized: “For every Lombardi or Bobby Knight you give me, I can give you an equally successful—if not more successful—humanistic coach… Despite the success of Wooden, Shula, Dungy, Stevens, and others, our society has conditioned us to think that autocratic coaches are better coaches; that they win more often. It’s a myth. But it’s a vicious cycle.”

In 2008 Eastern Washington researchers studied nearly two hundred basketball players and coaches and concluded: “The results of this study seem to suggest that the ‘keys’ to promoting mental toughness do not lie in this autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive style. It appears to lie, paradoxically, with the coach’s ability to produce an environment, which emphasizes trust and inclusion, humility, and service.”

TOUGHNESS MAXIM: Real toughness is experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It’s navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can.

## Searching for Real Toughness
The author recounts the Don Bowden Mile. In 1957 Bowden became the first American to break the four-minute mile. Fifty years later seven men lined up, six Cal blue and gold, one Houston red and white. The author charged to third behind rabbits, planning to zone out then reengage over the final lap. First lap 60 seconds. At halfway a coach yelled “1:59…2:00.”

Every runner has a fatigue tell. The author’s weak point was legs; breathing stayed rhythmic. At 900 meters a neck tightening and a high-pitched gasp like water down the wrong tube shattered autopilot. “What was that? What’s wrong? Why am I breathing hard? This is too soon. My legs feel fine. You’re done.” He tried tricks: breaking the race, ignoring fatigue, pushing through. He thought toughness got him there. Less than 100 meters later: “I can’t breathe. What the hell!? I can’t breathe!” He pulled off, collapsed on knees, then the blockage cleared.

He prided himself on toughness, throwing up after races. Coach Theresa Fuqua said: “You race with intensity. There’s never a question of whether the effort will be there or not; it’s just whether or not the body is going to produce what your mind wills it that day.”

Tests led to diagnosis by Dr. Stephen Miles: paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction. Vocal cords open on inhalation, partially close on exhalation, and protect airways. In VCD they malfunction, shutting when they should open, blocking airways. The theory is hyperresponsive cords like a trigger-happy guard. Severe cases cause inability to breathe in, with panic and anxiety. American Thoracic Society cites strong emotions and stress as triggers.

For years the sport he loved became feared. Pushing until he puked backfired. He had to relax breathing, neck and mind under control at peak discomfort. The book started at that collapse, a search for what toughness means and how to control an inner world that goes haywire.

Running anchors the book because it is alone, in your head, navigating immense discomfort. Lessons apply beyond sport to parenting, grief, leading people six to sixty. Real toughness makes you healthier and happier, teaching preparation, communication, response, transcendence of discomfort. The four pillars follow: Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality; Listen to Your Body; Respond Instead of React; Transcend Discomfort.

To continue sport, had to find new tactic: relax, keep breathing, neck, mind steady and under control at exact moment discomfort and doubts were highest. Book started the moment he collapsed. * Negative conditional regard
* Intimidation and isolation
* Excessive personal control

When researchers looked at ability to persist in various domains—cycling, math, calling for donations—one factor kept popping up. Those who persisted had different goals. Not driven by fear, guilt, pressure. Didn’t keep working for money. Pursued goal because it aligned with who they were and brought enjoyment and contentment. Choosing to do work, not forced. And they were having more success.

In studies spanning exercise and work, inner drive led to more effort, higher commitment, better results. Study of over one hundred British athletes found inner drive not only resulted in better persistence on demanding exercise test, but also helped with other toughness aspects: seeing challenge instead of threat and using positive coping strategies instead of dissociative or disengagement. Internally driven athletes experienced more positive emotions and increased willingness to repeat task after completion.

Tough decision: persist, sapping energy before riskiest part? Or abandon goal and find new one: making it down?

Tough individuals possess self-awareness to evaluate and weigh contrasting pulls of desire to continue and reality of demands and risks, to make best choice. Instead of blindly persisting, if right move is “quit,” they reframe goal or find new one and reengage. Climber’s goal shifts from reaching peak to returning safely. Inner drive brings clarity, allowing listening to body to make right decision during difficult moments. Whether goal is improve persistence or develop ability to reengage once goal seems lost, motivation from within appears special sauce. Psychologists call it autonomous motivation.

### Filling basic needs: self-determination theory

In 1970s, Edward Deci and colleagues gave what appeared to be wooden three-dimensional Tetris pieces to 24 college students and told them to build a shape. For three days, students returned to lab, shown new shape. For half, day two brought monetary reward per puzzle solved in allotted time. When participants returned day three, monetary reward was gone. Back to making shapes for sake of making shapes. With external incentive gone, motivation dropped. Participants spent less time attempting new shapes and were more apt to quit. Phenomenon now known as extrinsic vs intrinsic motivation was born. Other scientists repeated experiment in range of tasks and age groups. Before long, researchers replicated effect in schoolchildren drawing and athletes playing sports. When external reward or punishment introduced, it shifted motivational habits.

Deci, with psychologist Richard Ryan, had radical idea. Findings on what motivated people didn’t apply just to homework or solving problem, but to something greater: well-being. Deci and Ryan expanded work on intrinsic motivation, declaring we all have three basic and innate psychological needs. If satisfied, well-being improves, we’re self-motivated for growth and development. Self-determination theory (SDT) was born. Includes need for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Or, to feel in control, like you can make progress, and to belong.

Since introduction, SDT investigated and applied to parenting, teaching, substance abuse. Supporting Deci and Ryan’s hypothesis, needs satisfaction is linked to better health, ratings of well-being, performance in variety of domains. Autonomy, competence, relatedness serve as basic psychological needs. Fulfilling basic needs helps not only well-being but ability to persist.

## Organizing: Setting Up the Right Buckets

An airtight organization system lets the mind let go of lower-level thinking and graduate to intuitive focusing, undistracted by matters that haven’t been dealt with appropriately. The physical system must be better than the mental one. Airtight organization is required for focus to remain on the broader horizon and eliminate constant pressure to remember or be reminded.

Being organized means where something is matches what it means to you. If you decide you want to keep something as reference and you put it where reference material needs to be, that’s organized. If you think you need a reminder about a call you need to make, as long as you put that reminder where you want reminders of phone calls to make, you’re organized. It begs the question: What does something mean to you? Much of what people are trying to organize has not been clarified. Even once it has, more refined distinctions add greater creativity and control.

I must Create a System or be enslav’ d by another Man’s.

The outer ring of the Workflow Diagram shows the main groupings into which things will go as you decide what they are and what needs to be done about them.

### The Basic Categories

There are seven primary types of things to keep track of and manage:

* A Projects list
* Project support material
* Calendar actions and information
* Next Actions lists
* A Waiting For list
* Reference material
* A Someday/Maybe list

### Hard Edges

It’s critical that all categories be kept pristinely distinct. They each represent a discrete type of agreement we make with ourselves, to be reminded at a specific time and in a specific way, and if they lose their edges and blend, much of the value of organizing is lost.

The categories must be kept visually, physically, and psychologically separate, to promote clarity. If you allow things of different meanings into the same grouping, you will tend to go psychologically numb to the contents. If you put reference materials in the same pile as things you still want to read, you’ll go unconscious to the stack. If you put items on Next Actions lists that really need to go on the calendar because they have to occur on specific days, you won’t trust your calendar and you’ll continually reassess your action lists. If you have projects you’re not going to be doing anything about for some time, they must go on your Someday/Maybe list so you can relate to the Projects list with rigorous action-generating focus. And if something you’re Waiting For is included on an action list, nonproductive rethinking will continually bog you down.

### Lists and Folders

Once you know what you need to keep track of, all you really need are lists and folders—totally sufficient tools for reminders, reference, and support materials. Lists will keep track of projects and someday/maybes, as well as actions on active open loops. Folders will hold reference material and support information for active projects.

I would not give a fig for the simplicity on this side of complexity, but I would give my life for the simplicity on the other side of complexity.

You shouldn’t bother to create external structuring of priorities on your lists that you’ll then have to rearrange as things change. Attempting to impose such scaffolding has been a big source of frustration. You’ll prioritize more intuitively as you see the whole list against shifting variables. The list is just a way to keep track of the total inventory of active things to which you have made a commitment, and to have that inventory available for review.

### Organizing Action Reminders

If you’ve emptied your in-tray, you’ll have a stack of Pending reminders for longer-than-two-minute actions that cannot be delegated. You’ll probably have twenty to sixty or seventy or more such items.

#### Calendar actions

There are two basic kinds of actions: those that must be done on a certain day and/or at a particular time, and those that just need to be done as soon as you can get to them.

The calendar should show only the “hard landscape” around which you do the rest of your actions.

Calendared items can be time specific e.g., “10:00–11:00 meet with Jim” or day specific “Call Rachel Tuesday to see if she got the proposal”. Resist putting actions on the calendar that you think you’d really like to get done next Monday but that actually might not. You need to trust your calendar as sacred territory, reflecting the exact hard edges of your day’s commitments.

#### Context

The best way to be reminded of an “as soon as I can” action is by the particular context required—that is, tool, location or situation needed to complete it. If the action requires a computer, it should go on an At Computer list. If it demands you be out moving around, the Errands list is appropriate. If the next step is to talk face-to-face with your partner Emily, putting it into an “Emily” folder or list makes sense.

How discrete categories need to be depends on how many actions you have to track and how often you change contexts. If you have only twenty-five next actions, a single Next Actions list might suffice, with items as diverse as “Buy nails,” “Talk to boss about staff changes,” and “Draft ideas about committee meeting.” If you have fifty or a hundred pending, one big list makes it too difficult to see what you need to see.

#### Common categories

* Calls — all phone calls you need to make; record the phone number alongside each item.
* At Computer — actions you need to do when it’s on and running. Because I fly a lot, I maintain an Online action list separate from At Computer. When I’m on a plane without Wi-Fi I can’t connect to the Web or servers, so I can trust none of my At Computer actions require connection.
* Errands — things you need to do when out and about. Actions like “Get stock certificates from bank deposit box,” “Pick up suit at the tailor,” and “Buy flowers for Robyn at the florist” go here.
* At Office — things you can do only there.
* At Home — actions that can be done only at home: “Hang new watercolor print,” “Organize travel accessories,” and “Switch closets to winter clothes.” “At Starbucks” can be a fine categorization.
* Anywhere
* Agendas — next actions that need to occur in real-time interaction with someone or be brought up in a meeting. Put them on separate Agenda lists for each person and meeting.
* Read/Review — printed items that demand more than two minutes are best managed in a separate physical stack tray labeled “Read/Review.”

We must strive to reach that simplicity that lies beyond sophistication.

### Organizing Waiting For

Reminders of things you’re waiting to get back from or get done by others have to be sorted and grouped. You’re tracking final deliverables or projects others are responsible for, such as tickets ordered from the theater, the scanner coming for the office, the OK on the proposal from your client.

Manage the commitments of others before their avoidance creates a crisis.

For many in managerial positions, getting this inventory captured, current, complete, and reviewed creates tremendous relief and improved focus. Include the date each item is requested for, as well as any agreed-upon due date.

### Original Item as Reminder

The most efficient way to track action reminders is to add them to lists or folders as they occur. Certain kinds of input will most efficiently serve as their own reminders rather than writing something on a list.

Managing paper-based workflow: Read/Review articles, publications and documents is a good example. It would be overkill to write “Review Vogue magazine” on an action list when you can toss the magazine into your Read/Review tray.

The primary reason for organizing is to reduce cognitive load—i.e. to eliminate the need to constantly be thinking, “what do i need to do about this?”

Managing e-mail-based workflow: Create one folder for longer-than-two-minute e-mails you need to act on. The folder name should begin with a prefix letter or symbol so it looks different from reference folders and sits at the top. Use @ or hyphen. Your resulting @ACTION folder will hold e-mails you need to do something about. Create a folder titled “@WAITING FOR,” which will show up with @ACTION.

It takes much less energy to maintain e-mail backlog at zero than at a thousand.

Paper-based data is sometimes easier to trust for utility than digital versions. Distributing action triggers in a folder, on lists, and/or in an e-mail system is OK as long as you review all categories equally as required.

### Organizing Project Reminders

Creating and maintaining one list of all your projects can be a profound experience. You probably have more than you think.

The Projects list is not meant to hold plans or details, nor should you try to keep it arranged by priority or size or urgency—it’s just a comprehensive index of your open loops.

The real value lies in the complete review it can provide, ensuring you have action steps defined for all projects and nothing slips through the cracks. A complete and current Projects list is the major operational tool for moving from tree-hugging to forest management.

Value of a complete Projects list: Critical for control and focus; alleviates subtle tensions; core of the Weekly Review; facilitates relationship management.

Where to look for hidden projects: Current activities; Higher-horizon interests and commitments; Current problems, issues, and opportunities.

Most people find one list best because it serves as a master inventory rather than daily prioritizing guideline. Common subsorts: Personal/Professional; Delegated Projects; Specific Types of Projects.

The right amount of complexity is whatever creates optimal simplicity.

What about subprojects? If you’re moving into a new residence, you may have actionable items like “Finalize the patio,” “Upgrade the kitchen,” “Set up home office space.” Don’t be too concerned. If unsure, put big projects on the Projects list and hold subpieces in project support material, making sure to include them in Weekly Review.

As I write this, I’m in the throes of moving from California to Europe. For many months, I maintained one project on my Projects list: “Move to Amsterdam.” Last week, as things became more immediate, I unpacked that one project into fifteen—all of which I need to keep my eyes on weekly now, ranging from “Set up Dutch bank accounts” to “Finalize artwork storage in Santa Barbara.”

### Project Support Materials

Project support materials are not project actions, and they’re not project reminders. They’re resources to support actions and thinking about projects.

Don’t use support material for reminding. People use stacks of paper, stuffed file folders, and e-mails as reminders they’ve got a project and have to do something about it. Next actions and Waiting For items have usually not been determined and are psychologically still embedded in the stacks.

What continues to talk to you psychologically in your environment, demanding that you do something about it?

There is no need ever to lose an idea about a project, theme, or topic.

### Organizing Nonactionable Data

Nonactionable items fall into three large categories: reference materials, reminders of things that need no action now but might at a later date, and things you don’t need at all.

#### Reference materials

Much of what comes across your desk is reference material. There’s no action required, but it’s information you want to keep.

Your reference and filing system should be a simple library of data, easily retrievable—not your reminder for actions, projects, priorities, or prospects.

If material is purely for reference, the only issue is whether it’s worth the time and space to keep it.

#### Someday/Maybe

Someday/Maybes are not throwaway items. They may be some of the most interesting and creative things you’ll ever get involved with.

Examples: “Learn Spanish,” “Get Marcie a horse,” “Climb Mt. Washington,” “Write a mystery novel,” and “Get a vacation cottage.”

Activating and maintaining your someday/Maybe category unleashes the flow of your creative thinking—you have permission to imagine cool things to do without having to commit to doing anything about them yet.

The danger of “Hold and Review” files and piles: Many people create a “Hold and Review” pile and tell themselves, “When I have time, I may like to get to this.” I personally don’t recommend this subsystem, because in virtually every case the person held but didn’t review, and there was numbness and resistance about the stack.

What lies in our power to do, lies in our power not to do.

It’s oK to decide not to decide—as long as you have a decide-not-to-decide system.

#### Tickler file

Essentially the tickler file is a simple file-folder system that allows you to distribute paper and other physical reminders so whatever you want to see on a particular date in the future “automatically” shows up that day in your in-tray.

Setting up a tickler file requires forty-three folders—thirty-one labeled “1” through “31,” and twelve more labeled with the names of the months.

Bottom line: the tickler file demands only a one-second-per-day new behavior to make it work, and it has a payoff value exponentially greater than the personal investment.

### Checklists

Checklists are “recipes of potential ingredients” for projects, work processes and procedures, events, and areas of value, interest, and responsibility.

Things you want to pay attention to often show up as: Exercise more regularly; Spend more quality time with my kids; Do more proactive planning for my division; Maintain good morale on my team.

First, identify inherent projects and action. For much of this stuff, there is still a project and/or an action that needs to be defined.

Blueprinting key areas of work and accountability: Objectives like “Maintain good physical conditioning” or “Keep my team motivated” may still need to be built into some sort of overview checklist reviewed regularly.

The more novel the situation, the more control required. The degree to which any of us needs to maintain checklists and external controls is directly related to our unfamiliarity with the area of responsibility.

Checklists can be highly useful to let you know what you need to be concerned about.

Be open to creating any kind of checklist as the urge strikes you. Capability and willingness to instantly make a checklist, accessible and used when needed, is a core component of high-performance self-management.

For organization, there are two basic kinds of actions: those that must be done on a certain day and/or at a particular time, and those that just need to be done as soon as you can get to them, around your other calendar items.

The calendar should show only the “hard landscape” around which you do the rest of your actions.

Calendared action items can be either time specific e.g., “10:00–11:00 meet with Jim” or day specific “Call Rachel Tuesday to see if she got the proposal”.

Resist putting actions on the calendar that you think you’d really like to get done next Monday, say, but that actually might not. You need to trust your calendar as sacred territory, reflecting the exact hard edges of your day’s commitments, which should be noticeable at a glance while you’re on the run.

Organizing As-Soon-As-Possible Actions by Context

The best way to be reminded of an “as soon as I can” action is by the particular context required for that action—that is, either the tool or the location or the situation needed to complete it. For instance, if the action requires a computer, it should go on an At Computer list. If your action demands that you be out and moving around in the world, the Errands list would be the appropriate place to track it. If the next step is to talk about something face-to-face with your partner, Emily, putting it into an “Emily” folder or list makes the most sense.

How discrete these categories will need to be will depend on how many actions you actually have to track; and how often you change the contexts within which to do them.

If you have only twenty-five next actions, a single Next Actions list might suffice. It could include items as diverse as “Buy nails,” “Talk to boss about staff changes,” and “Draft ideas about committee meeting.” If, however, you have fifty or a hundred next actions pending, keeping all of those on one big list would make it too difficult to see what you need to see.

The Most Common Categories of Action Reminders

* Calls
* At Computer
* Errands
* At Office
* At Home
* Anywhere
* Agendas
* Read/Review

Calls. This is the list of all the phone calls you need to make; you can work off it as long as you have a phone available. I suggest that you take the time to record the phone number alongside each item.

At Computer. If you work with a computer, it can be helpful to group all those actions that you need to do when it’s on and running. Because I fly a lot, I maintain an Online action list, separate from my At Computer one. When I’m on a plane without a Wi-Fi service I can’t connect to the Web or my servers, as many actions require. So instead of having to rethink what I can and can’t do whenever I look at my At Computer list, I can trust that none of my At Computer actions require that I be connected.

Errands. It makes a lot of sense to group together in one place reminders of all the things you need to do when you’re out and about. Actions like “Get stock certificates from bank deposit box,” “Pick up suit at the tailor,” and “Buy flowers for Robyn at the florist” would all go here.

We must strive to reach that simplicity that lies beyond sophistication.

At Office. If you work in an office, there will be certain things that you can do only there, and a list of those things will be useful to have in front of you then.

At Home. Many actions can be done only at home, and it makes sense to keep a list specific to that context. “Hang new watercolor print,” “Organize travel accessories,” and “Switch closets to winter clothes” would be typical items for this grouping. “At Starbucks” can be a fine categorization for an action list!

Agendas. Invariably you’ll find that many of your next actions need to either occur in a real-time interaction with someone or be brought up in a committee, team, or staff meeting. These next actions should be put on separate Agenda lists for each of those people and for that meeting.

Read/Review. To-read printed items that you know will demand more than two minutes of your time are usually best managed in a separate physical stack tray labeled “Read/Review.”

Those who make the worst use of their time are the first to complain of its shortness.

Organizing “Waiting For”

Like reminders of the actions you need to do, reminders of all the things that you’re waiting to get back from or get done by others have to be sorted and grouped. You won’t necessarily be tracking discrete action steps here, but more often final deliverables or projects that others are responsible for, such as the tickets you’ve ordered from the theater, the scanner that’s coming for the office, the OK on the proposal from your client, and so on.

Manage the commitments of others before their avoidance creates a crisis.

For many people, especially those in managerial or supervisory positions, getting this inventory of unfulfilled commitments that we care about from others captured, current, complete, and reviewed creates tremendous relief and improved focus going forward.

It’s important for this category in particular to include the date that each item is requested for each entry, as well as any agreed-upon due date.

Using the Original Item as Its Own Action Reminder

The most efficient way to track your action reminders is to add them to lists or folders as they occur to you. There are some exceptions to this rule, however. Certain kinds of input will most efficiently serve as their own reminders of required actions, rather than your having to write something about them on a list.

Managing Paper-Based Workflow

Some things are their own best reminders of work to be done. The category of Read/Review articles, publications, and documents is a good example. It would obviously be overkill to write “Review Vogue magazine” on some action list when you could just as easily toss the magazine itself into your Read/Review tray to act as the trigger.

The primary reason for organizing is to reduce cognitive load—i.e. to eliminate the need to constantly be thinking, “what do i need to do about this?”

Whichever option you select, the reminders should be in visibly discrete categories based upon the next action required.

Managing E-mail-Based Workflow

E-mails that need action are sometimes best as their own reminders—in this case within the e-mail system itself. Create one folder for any longer-than-two-minute e-mails that you need to act on. The folder name should begin with a prefix letter or symbol so that it looks different from your reference folders and sits at the top of your folders in the navigator bar. Use something like the @ sign or the hyphen. Your resulting @ACTION folder will hold those e-mails that you need to do something about.

Next you can create a folder titled “@WAITING FOR,” which will show up in the same place as the @ACTION folder.

It takes much less energy to maintain e-mail backlog at zero than at a thousand.

Getting E-mail “In” to Empty

The method detailed above will enable you to actually get everything out of your e-mail in-tray, which will be a huge boon to your clarity about, and control of, your day-to-day work.

A Caution About Dispersing Reminders of Your Actions

There’s an obvious danger in putting reminders of things you need to do somewhere out of sight. The function of an organization system is primarily to supply the reminders you need to see when you need to see them, so you can trust your choices about what you’re doing.

Paper-based data is sometimes easier to trust for utility than digital versions.

Distributing action triggers in a folder, on lists, and/or in an e-mail system is perfectly OK, as long as you review all of the categories to which you’ve entrusted your triggers equally, as required.

### Organizing Project Reminders

Creating and maintaining one list of all your projects can be a profound experience! You probably have more of them than you think.

The Projects List(s)

The Projects list is not meant to hold plans or details about your projects themselves, nor should you try to keep it arranged by priority or size or urgency—it’s just a comprehensive index of your open loops.

The real value of the Projects list lies in the complete review it can provide, ensuring that you have action steps defined for all of your projects and that nothing is slipping through the cracks.

A complete and current Projects list is the major operational tool for moving from tree-hugging to forest management.

The Value of a Complete Projects List

* Critical for control and focus
* Alleviates subtle tensions
* Core of the Weekly Review
* Facilitates relationship management

Projects seldom show up in nice, neat packages. small things often slip unexpectedly into bigger things.

Where to Look for Projects Still to Uncover

* Current activities
* Higher-horizon interests and commitments
* Current problems, issues, and opportunities

Current Activities. Often there are projects that need to be captured from a simple inventory of your calendar, your action lists, and your workspaces.

One List, or Subdivided?

Most people find that one list is the best way to go because it serves as a master inventory rather than as a daily prioritizing guideline.

Some Common Ways to Subsort Projects

Personal/Professional. Many people feel more comfortable seeing their lists divided up between personal and professional projects.

Delegated Projects. If you’re a senior manager or executive, you probably have several projects that you are directly responsible for but have handed off to people who report to you.

Specific Types of Projects. Some people have as part of their work and lifestyle several different projects of the same type, which in some instances it may be valuable to group together as a sub-list of Projects.

The right amount of complexity is whatever creates optimal simplicity.

What About Subprojects?

Some of your projects will likely have major subprojects, each of which could in theory be seen as a whole project. If you’re moving into a new residence, for instance, and are upgrading or changing much of what’s there, you may have a list of actionable items like “Finalize the patio,” “Upgrade the kitchen,” “Set up home office space,” and so on.

Don’t be too concerned about which way is best. If you’re not sure, I’d vote for putting your big projects on the Projects list and holding the subpieces in your project support material, making sure to include them in your Weekly Review.

As I write this, I’m in the throes of moving from California to Europe. For many months, I maintained one project on my Projects list: “Move to Amsterdam.” Last week, as things became more immediate and necessary to deal with on multiple fronts, I unpacked that one project into fifteen—all of which I need to keep my eyes on weekly now, ranging from “Set up Dutch bank accounts” to “Finalize artwork storage in Santa Barbara.”

Project Support Materials

Project support materials are not project actions, and they’re not project reminders. They’re resources to support your actions and thinking about your projects.

Don’t Use Support Material for Reminding. Typically, people use stacks of paper, stuffed file folders, and/or a plethora of e-mails and digital documents as reminders that they’ve got a project, and they’ve got to do something about it.

What continues to talk to you psychologically in your environment, demanding that you do something about it?

Organizing Ad Hoc Project Thinking

In chapter 3, it was suggested that you will often have ideas that you’ll want to keep about projects but that are not necessarily next actions. Those ideas fall into the broad category of “project support materials.”

There is no need ever to lose an idea about a project, theme, or topic.

### Organizing Nonactionable Data

Nonactionable items fall into three large categories: reference materials, reminders of things that need no action now but might at a later date, and things that you don’t need at all.

Reference Materials

Much of what comes across your desk and into your life in general is reference material. There’s no action required, but it’s information that you want to keep.

The Variety of Reference Systems

* General-reference filing—paper, e-mail, and simple digital storage
* Large-category filing
* Contact managers
* Libraries and archives

Your reference and filing system should be a simple library of data, easily retrievable—not your reminder for actions, projects, priorities, or prospects.

If material is purely for reference, the only issue is whether it’s worth the time and space to keep it.

Someday/Maybes

The second thing to deal with in organizing nonactionable items is how to track things that you want to reassess in the future.

Someday/Maybes are not throwaway items. They may be some of the most interesting and creative things you’ll ever get involved with.

Someday/Maybe List

It’s highly likely that if you did a complete mind sweep when you were collecting things from your mental space, you came up with some things you’re not sure you want to commit to. “Learn Spanish,” “Get Marcie a horse,” “Climb Mt. Washington,” “Write a mystery novel,” and “Get a vacation cottage” are typical projects that fall into this category.

Activating and maintaining your someday/Maybe category unleashes the flow of your creative thinking—you have permission to imagine cool things to do without having to commit to doing anything about them yet.

Special Categories of Someday/Maybe

More than likely you have some special interests that involve lots of possible things to do. It can be fun to collect these on lists.

The Danger of “Hold and Review” Files and Piles

Many people have created some sort of “Hold and Review” pile or file that vaguely fits within the category of Someday/Maybe. They tell themselves, “When I have time, I may like to get to this,” and a “Hold and Review” file seems a convenient place to put it. I personally don’t recommend this particular kind of subsystem, because in virtually every case I have come across, the person held but didn’t review, and there was numbness and resistance about the stack and contents.

What lies in our power to do, lies in our power not to do.

Using the Calendar for Future Options

Your calendar can be a very handy place to park reminders of things you might want to consider doing in the future.

* Triggers for Activating Projects
* Events you might want to participate in
* Decision catalysts

It’s oK to decide not to decide—as long as you have a decide-not-to-decide system.

The “Tickler” File

One elegant way to manage nonactionable items that may need an action in the future is the tickler file. Essentially the tickler file is a simple file-folder system that allows you to distribute paper and other physical reminders in such a way that whatever you want to see on a particular date in the future “automatically” shows up that day in your in-tray.

Setting Up a Tickler File

If you are doing this in a physical system, you need forty-three folders—thirty-one labeled “1” through “31,” and twelve more labeled with the names of the months of the year.

Bottom line: the tickler file demands only a one-second-per-day new behavior to make it work, and it has a payoff value exponentially greater than the personal investment.

### Checklists: Creative and Constructive Reminders

The last topic in personal system organization that deserves some attention is the care and feeding of checklists, those “recipes of potential ingredients” for projects, work processes and procedures, events, and areas of value, interest, and responsibility.

Things You Want to Pay Attention To

Often, when we are working with people to clear up what is on their minds, what shows up are things like: Exercise more regularly; Spend more quality time with my kids; Do more proactive planning for my division; Maintain good morale on my team.

First, Identify Inherent Projects and Action

For much of this kind of stuff, there is still a project and/or an action that needs to be defined.

Blueprinting Key Areas of Work and Accountability

Objectives like “Maintain good physical conditioning” or “Keep my team motivated” may still need to be built into some sort of overview checklist that will be reviewed regularly.

The More Novel the Situation, the More Control Required

The degree to which any of us needs to maintain checklists and external controls is directly related to our unfamiliarity with the area of responsibility.

Checklists can be highly useful to let you know what you need to be concerned about.

Checklists at All Levels

Be open to creating any kind of checklist as the urge strikes you. The possibilities are endless—from “Core Life Values” to “Things to Take Camping” to “Potential Holiday Gifts.”

Capability and willingness to instantly make a checklist, accessible and used when needed, is a core component of high-performance self-management.

: ## Chapter 6: The Formula of Humanity

### Kant as a productivity machine
Immanuel Kant woke at five, wrote three hours, lectured four hours, ate lunch at the same restaurant, walked the same park route leaving and returning at the same time, and went to bed at ten for forty years. Neighbors joked they could set clocks by his 3:30 walk. From a single-room apartment in Königsberg, Prussia, he argued for inherent human dignity, first envisioned a global governing body that would inspire the United Nations, helped inspire Einstein’s relativity, suggested animal rights, reinvented aesthetics, resolved rationalism vs empiricism, and reinvented moral philosophy. He lived a rigid, uncompromising value system outside Feeling Brain judgments; kings censored him, priests condemned him, academics envied him. He eschewed hope and the flawed values it relies on, confronted the Uncomfortable Truth, and stood before the gods with logic.

### How to Grow Up
A four-year-old learns hot stoves burn and ice cream is pleasurable; the meta-lesson is a value judgment: ice cream is better than being burned. The Feeling Brain builds an early value hierarchy by collecting what pleases and harms. Exploration exhausts because the world is too vast; the two brains develop rules to navigate complexity, often adopted from parents and teachers. After enough near-flames, “all flames are dangerous” forms; after punishment, raiding the freezer is always bad. Abstract principles emerge: take care around danger; be honest; share.

A child’s identity is pleasure and pain: Susie likes chocolate, fears dogs, enjoys coloring, is mean to her brother. Adolescence keeps pleasure/pain but adds if/then rules and cause-effect chains. The adolescent weighs feelings against rules, trade-offs, and social order, gaining a sturdier identity. The adolescent tries social roles: “If I wear this, will I be cool?” Life becomes bargains: do what the boss says for money; call mother to avoid yelling; do homework to avoid future harm; lie to avoid conflict. Nothing is done for its own sake; everything is a means to a pleasurable end. Adolescent values never stand for something outside the self; they maximize pleasure and minimize pain with foresight.

### How to Be an Adult
Adulthood is acting on an abstract principle for its own sake, even if it hurts. The adolescent values honesty for results and lies when convenient; the adult is honest because honesty is inherently good, an end not a means. The adolescent loves as an emotional swap meet; the adult loves freely without expectation. Adult values are unconditional ends in themselves. Maturity is about why you act, not age. The child steals for pleasure; the adolescent refrains to avoid future pain; the adult doesn’t steal because stealing is wrong and would make her feel worse.

### Why We Don’t Grow
Children transcend pleasure/pain values by experiencing their failure. Good parenting implements correct consequences: punish stealing ice cream, reward sitting quietly. Without predictable consequences, the child realizes the world does not cater to whims; learning this late is painful. Abuse also stalls development: punishment is random and cruel, no lesson is learned, no higher values form. Coddled and abused children often remain stuck in childhood values.

Graduating to adolescence requires trust in predictable outcomes. A society without trustworthy institutions devolves into childish selfishness. People get stuck in adolescent values via trauma or neglect; bullied people assume affection must be hard-won through practiced actions. Some become skilled manipulators, believing life is a high-school gymnasium where you must shove others into lockers. Teaching unconditionality requires example: trust the adolescent to teach trust; respect to teach respect; love to teach love, without making it conditional.

When parents and teachers are stuck at adolescent values, they bargain love for sex, loyalty for affection, respect for obedience, replicating transactional relationships. Adolescent-minded adults assume all relationships are trade agreements and blame transaction technique rather than the transactional approach. Acting unconditionally requires faith that it is right even if it causes pain. Adult behaviors are admirable: the boss who takes the fall, the mother who gives up happiness for her child, the friend who tells hard truths.

Religions push unconditional values—unconditional forgiveness, the Noble Eightfold Path, perfect justice—but are co-opted by transactional adolescents and narcissistic children. Enlightenment philosophers created ideological religions focused on measurable goals: greater happiness, liberties, compassion, equality. These also caved to conditionality: bartering for happiness destroys happiness; enforcing freedom negates freedom; creating equality undermines equality. Whatever the God Value, people will bargain away human life to achieve it, restarting the hope-destruction cycle. This is where Kant comes in.

### The One Rule for Life
Kant observed consciousness is scarce and unique: we can reason and improve the world; we are the only known source of ingenuity, self-awareness, and self-organization. The supreme value is the thing that conceives value itself; the ability to form meaning is the only force that can propagate intelligence and generate greater organization. Without rationality, the universe would be rocks. Consciousness can reorganize the universe exponentially.

Kant’s fundamental moral duty is preservation and growth of consciousness in self and others. He called this “the Formula of Humanity”: “Act that you use humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, always at the same time as an end, never merely as a means.” It pulls people from adolescent bargaining into adult virtue, explains moral intuitions, virtue, and daily action without hope.

Hope is transactional: don’t eat this, you’ll go to heaven; work hard for happiness. Transcending hope requires unconditional action: love without expectation, respect without expectation, honesty without reward. Treat humanity never merely as a means but always as an end itself.

Means are done conditionally; ends are desired for their own sake. Eating a burrito is an end; driving and paying gas are means. If the burrito is for a wife’s happiness, the burrito is a means to a greater end. Treating a wife as a means to sex is wrong. Lying, cheating, violence treat others as means to one’s own ends. Honesty is good because it doesn’t use people as means; courage is good because failing to act treats self/others as means to quell fear; humility is good because blind certainty treats others as means.

The Formula does not rely on hope or utopia; it respects and protects conscious will. Improving the world is improving ourselves by treating self and others as ends: be honest, don’t harm self, don’t shirk responsibility, love openly, don’t cave to tribal impulses. There is no heaven or hell, only moment-to-moment choices.

Self-respect links to respect for the world. Pursuing pleasure treats self as a means. Self-improvement is cultivation of self-respect: telling yourself you are worthless is as wrong as telling others; lying to self is as unethical as lying to others; harming self is as repugnant as harming others. The Formula has a ripple effect: honesty with self increases honesty with others, enabling maturation.

Changing the world is maturation and dignity in the present, not ideology or mass conversion. Dignity and respect in each moment must be universal.

### The Modern Maturity Crisis
Modern democracy assumes the average person is selfish and delusional; it protects via interlocking systems so no group can hose the rest. Politics is transactional; democracy admits this and enshrines adult virtues in design: free speech, free press, privacy, fair trial. These implement the Formula of Humanity and are hard to threaten.

Democracy is threatened when a group subverts it with another religion and political extremism grows. Extremists are childish: intractable, refusing negotiation or higher virtue, untrustworthy. The most dangerous dress childish values in transactional or universal language. A right-wing extremist claims freedom but wants freedom from other values, willing to limit others’ freedom. A left extremist claims equality but wants no one to feel pain, willing to cause pain to eliminate moral gaps.

Extremism has grown for decades. The author suggests cultural maturity is deteriorating. The rich world faces not a material crisis but a crisis of character, virtue, means and ends. The 21st-century schism is maturity vs immaturity, means vs ends, not right vs left or communism vs capitalism.

Pilecki fought against both Germans and Soviets and after defeat formed the Secret Polish Army in Warsaw. By summer 1940 thousands of military officers and leading Polish nationals were disappearing from western Poland. Better talent also arrived at A&M; Bryant admitted, “That first year was brutal. We could hardly get anybody to come to A&M, and I know some of our alumni went out and paid a few boys.”

The camp was sorting, “separating the wheat from the chaff,” not development. Top recruits quit, including All-Southwest Conference Fred Broussard, who played in the NFL, and Joe Boring, who switched to baseball and led the Aggies to a conference title. Foster “Tooter” Teague left camp due to injury and became a TOPGUN fighter in Vietnam, flying F-8 and F-4s, earning a Silver Star, commanding USS Kitty Hawk, and testing a Soviet MiG.

Survivors often stayed because they had no choice. Jack Pardee: “I never thought about quitting… If I did, where would I go?” Running back Bobby Drake Keith: “A lot has been made about the ones who stuck it out being stronger or whatever. But I think most of us survived because football was important to us for whatever reason, and it was in our nature to do whatever we had to do to stay on the team and stay in school. Our instinct was survival.”

Bryant later apologized at a twenty-five-year reunion, saying, “if it had been me, I’d have quit a dozen times, but they never quit. I didn’t know if I was doing it right or not, but it was the only way I knew how to do it.” The story became a Darwinian “sink or swim” model of toughness: siphon off the weak, harden the rest.

### Military toughness misread
Before coaching, Bryant served in the Navy in World War II. The common conception links military-style training to Junction-style toughness, but the military does not use boot camps to develop toughness; it uses them to sort. Sports took the sorting part as development and missed how the military actually builds resilience.

Navy SEALs’ “Hell Week” is designed to see who can survive war stress, not to toughen people. Under extreme stress many soldiers dissociate — amnesia, depersonalization, derealization — an involuntary coping strategy. Research found 96 percent of soldiers experience dissociative symptoms under extreme stress; 65 percent of experienced soldiers reported “lost track of what was going on”; all but two of ninety-four interviewed “felt as if they were looking at the world through a fog.”

Some soldiers stay engaged and keep cognitive wits despite the fog. The U.S. military needed to train that capacity.

After Korean War POW mass casualties, survival training became strategic. In 1961 the Air Force opened its first survival school; Navy and Army followed. The SERE program — Survival, Evasion, Resistance, and Escape — has three phases: classroom, evasion, and detention.

Evasion drops soldiers in wilderness to evade actors and live off land, then they are captured for detention: cells, periodic physical and psychological beatings, interrogations such as being stuffed into a box, with a blaring speaker described by a former Navy pilot as “A mind-numbing cacophony of an out-of-control saxophone was followed by Rudyard Kipling reciting his poem ‘Boots’ over and over in a very haunting voice.”

Detention is dreaded by trainees and romanticized outside. It works partly because the first, overlooked phase teaches skills first. The classroom phase is a barrage of lectures; the U.S. Air Force SERE operations manual is 652 pages covering psychological aspects of survival, medicine, camouflage, fire making, river hydraulics, handling boredom, loneliness, hopelessness, losing the will to survive, and over two dozen other maladies.

SERE is stress inoculation: vaccinate against extreme stress, but first teach coping skills. Without skills, the harrowing practice is useless; the inoculation must not overwhelm the system.

The military later moved beyond “make people do difficult things.” In 1989 the U.S. Military Academy introduced the Center for Enhanced Performance, teaching goal setting, positive self-talk, and stress management. Branches added mental skills coaching; as of 2018 the U.S. Army was the largest employer of sports psychologists.

In 2014 RAND asked, “Is the Air Force doing everything it can to prepare battlefield airmen to perform successfully under stressful conditions?” Top recommendations: emphasize core performance skills — confidence, goal setting, attention control, arousal control, imagery, self-talk, compartmentalization, mental skills foundation — and ensure those skills are mastered before stressful exposure. Early 2000s Navy SEALs added a classroom phase to train candidates to “monitor their psychological performance and learn to maximize mental toughness skills.”

Sports psychologist Brian Zuleger: “Telling people to relax doesn’t work unless you’ve taught people how to actually relax. The same goes for mental strength. The historical way to develop toughness was to do something physically challenging, and you’d have a fifty-fifty shot if they thrived. You have to teach the skill before it can be applied.”

The vaccine analogy extends to a robust immune system: specific inoculation helps, but a general resilience base helps with unfamiliar threats. Comprehensive Soldier Fitness aims to “maximize [a soldier’s] potential and face the physical and psychological challenges of sustained operations.” Strength-based psychological development draws from positive psychology — learned optimism, resilience, post-traumatic growth, emotion regulation — rather than only preparing for the worst. In 2015 the U.S. Army enacted the Human Dimension Strategy to develop the holistic person with objectives including intellectual optimization, social intelligence, holistic health and fitness, decision making, and team building.

The lesson taken from the military was wrong: it is not authoritarian control, discipline, or machismo. The sorting was mistaken for training; the teaching was glossed over. Toughness is not a sorting exercise; skills must be taught to handle adversity.

Researchers found soldiers who kept a clear head under extreme stress:
* appraised stress as a challenge instead of a threat, thanks in large part to a better assessment of what they encountered;
* utilized a diverse array of methods to cope with stress, demonstrating a high degree of cognitive flexibility;
* processed internal signals better, without reacting to them; and
* didn’t react to negative stimuli but instead were able to change their physiological state.

High performers navigate adversity with grit and grace rather than bulldozing through. Even the best want to quit under extreme discomfort; the author surveyed dozens of authors, entrepreneurs, executives, soldiers, and athletes who had moments of wanting to quit. Negative thoughts of quitting are normal, a protective signal.

### From discomfort to action
The chapter illustrates the cycle: Feel → Inner debate → Urge → Decision. Sensations and thoughts push toward a decision to quit, persist, or change goals. Sometimes the jump is direct from sensation to decision.

The brain functions to maintain order and reduce uncertainty, willing to minimize surprise even at high cost. When internal state is off-kilter, the brain seeks closure. Quitting can make the unknown known; changing expectations can pre-empt discomfort; exploring, accepting, or avoiding can restore order.

Toughness is making the pull for closure work with you, not against you — training the mind to tolerate uncertainty long enough to choose the “correct” response rather than the quickest. The book will unpack pillars that address the cycle from feeling to decision, starting with understanding why bulldozing often worsens outcomes.

## British Cycling and marginal gains

The fate of British Cycling changed in 2003 when Dave Brailsford was hired as performance director. Since 1908 British riders had won just a single Olympic gold medal and no Tour de France winner in 110 years; one top European bike manufacturer refused to sell bikes to the team for fear it would hurt sales.

Brailsford pursued “the aggregation of marginal gains,” the philosophy of searching for a tiny margin of improvement in everything. He said, “The whole principle came from the idea that if you broke down everything you could think of that goes into riding a bike, and then improve it by 1 percent, you will get a significant increase when you put them all together.”

Small adjustments included redesigning bike seats, rubbing alcohol on tires, electrically heated overshorts, biofeedback sensors, wind-tunnel fabric tests and switching to lighter indoor racing suits. Further 1 percent improvements were testing massage gels for recovery, a surgeon teaching hand-washing to reduce colds, determining optimal pillow and mattress for sleep, and painting the inside of the team truck white to spot dust that could degrade bikes.

After five years the team dominated Beijing 2008, winning an astounding 60 percent of the gold medals available in road and track cycling. In London 2012 they set nine Olympic records and seven world records. That year Bradley Wiggins became the first British cyclist to win the Tour de France; teammate Chris Froome won in 2013 and again in 2015, 2016 and 2017, giving Britain five Tour de France victories in six years. From 2007 to 2017 British cyclists won 178 world championships and sixty-six Olympic or Paralympic gold medals and five Tour de France victories.

## Why small habits make a big difference

It is easy to overestimate one defining moment and underestimate daily small improvements. Improving by 1 percent isn’t notable, but it can be far more meaningful long term. If you get 1 percent better each day for one year, you’ll end up thirty-seven times better; conversely, 1 percent worse each day declines nearly to zero. Habits are the compound interest of self-improvement.

Small changes seem to make little difference day to day, yet impact over months and years can be enormous. Saving a little money, going to the gym three days, or studying Mandarin for an hour do not produce immediate results, so people slide back. A single unhealthy meal or night of procrastination seems dismissible, but repeated 1 percent errors compound into toxic results.

A 3.5-degree heading shift on a Los Angeles to New York flight lands in Washington, D.C., instead of New York. A slight change in daily habits can guide life to a different destination. Success is the product of daily habits, not once-in-a-lifetime transformations.

It does not matter how successful or unsuccessful you are now; trajectory matters more than current results. Outcomes are lagging measures of habits: net worth lags financial habits, weight lags eating habits, knowledge lags learning habits, clutter lags cleaning habits. You get what you repeat. Time magnifies the margin between success and failure; good habits make time an ally, bad habits an enemy. Habits are a double-edged sword.

## What progress is really like

An ice cube at 25 degrees remains solid through 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31 degrees; at 32 degrees it melts. Breakthrough moments result from many prior actions that build potential. Cancer spends 80 percent of its life undetectable then takes over in months; bamboo builds roots for five years then explodes ninety feet in six weeks.

Habits appear to make no difference until a critical threshold is crossed. Early stages produce a Valley of Disappointment where progress feels linear and ineffective. The Plateau of Latent Potential is the period before visible change. Complaining about no success despite hard work is like complaining an ice cube has not melted from 25 to 31 degrees; work is stored. When the plateau is broken, the outside world calls it overnight success.

Mastery requires patience. The San Antonio Spurs display a quote from social reformer Jacob Riis: “When nothing seems to help, I go and look at a stonecutter hammering away at his rock, perhaps a hundred times without as much as a crack showing in it. Yet at the hundred and first blow it will split in two, and I know it was not that last blow that did it—but all that had gone before.”

All big things come from small beginnings. The seed of every habit is a single tiny decision; repeated, it sprouts and grows. Breaking a bad habit is like uprooting an oak; building a good habit is like cultivating a delicate flower one day at a time.

## Forget about goals, focus on systems instead

Prevailing wisdom says set specific, actionable goals. Clear once approached habits as goals and later realized results had little to do with goals and nearly everything to do with systems. Goals are about results you want; systems are about processes that lead to results, a distinction first learned from Scott Adams.

A coach’s goal is to win a championship; the system is recruiting, managing assistants, and practice. An entrepreneur’s goal is a million-dollar business; the system is testing ideas, hiring, marketing. A musician’s goal is to play a new piece; the system is practice frequency, breaking down measures, feedback.

If you ignored goals and focused only on the system, you would still succeed. The goal in sport is the best score, but staring at the scoreboard is ridiculous; you win by getting better each day. Bill Walsh: “The score takes care of itself.”

Goals are good for direction, but systems make progress. Problems arise when goals dominate:

* Winners and losers share goals. Survivorship bias focuses on winners. Every Olympian wants gold; the goal did not differentiate British cyclists. They won after implementing a system of continuous small improvements.
* Achieving a goal is momentary. A clean room returns to mess if sloppy habits remain. Results change temporarily; systems cause results. Fix inputs and outputs fix themselves.
* Goals restrict happiness. The assumption “once I reach my goal, then I’ll be happy” puts happiness off. Goals create either-or conflict. A systems-first mentality lets you be satisfied when the system runs, and success can take many forms.
* Goals create a yo-yo effect. Runners stop training after the race. The purpose of goals is to win the game; systems let you keep playing. True long-term thinking is goal-less thinking.

## A system of atomic habits

If you struggle to change habits, the problem is your system, not you. Bad habits repeat because the system for change is wrong. You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.

An atomic habit is a tiny change, a marginal gain, a 1 percent improvement, and part of a larger system. Atoms build molecules; atomic habits build remarkable results. Habits are the atoms of life.

* Habits are the compound interest of self-improvement. Getting 1 percent better every day counts for a lot long-run.
* Habits are a double-edged sword; they can work for or against you.
* Small changes appear to make no difference until a critical threshold is crossed; outcomes are delayed; patience is needed.
* An atomic habit is a little habit that is part of a larger system.
* For better results, focus on your system instead of setting goals.
* You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.
